name: Seam
label: Touch and Go
lede: Sooyoung Park left the noise of Bitch Magnet for something slower, made four records that a generation of emo bands wore out, and took his band to Seoul before almost any American indie act had tried.

eras.title: Out of Bitch Magnet, into Chapel Hill
eras.text: Sooyoung Park had already fronted Bitch Magnet at Oberlin, a loud, knotty band that pointed toward math rock. In Chapel Hill he turned the volume of his songs down and the weight up, with a bassist from home and a drummer borrowed from Superchunk.

years.h: Park, Lexi Mitchell and Mac McCaughan start Seam in Chapel Hill
years.p: Park moved to Chapel Hill with bassist Lexi Mitchell. [[Mac McCaughan|8841967d-3914-4ab9-aca6-94781aa35288]], who sang and played guitar in [[Superchunk|61653550-fd9b-4401-8248-44f2d064d384]], took the drum stool.
years.xp:
Park came out of [[Bitch Magnet|6be97715-b3fe-421b-b478-c4462ee9de15]], the Oberlin College band he co-founded in the 1980s. Their Star Booty EP was made with [[Steve Albini|a4d486bd-6020-4a36-9c7d-bf5ce174bcd1]], and Firebird credits the band with setting up a lot of the math rock and post-rock of the next decade.

Seam went the other way: slower songs, quieter verses, Park's voice up front. The debut single, "Days of Thunder", came out on Homestead in 1991.

years.h: Seam cuts Headsparks at Duck-Kee in Raleigh
years.p: Jerry Kee produces the session at his Raleigh studio. Homestead takes the record in the US and City Slang in Europe.
Thirty-three minutes of slow, fuzzed guitar songs, opening with "Decatur". Andrew Earles later called them "fuzzed-out downer anthems."
years.xp:
Earles heard the record as an advanced version of the melodic pieces that had broken up the more aggressive Bitch Magnet albums. AllMusic's Ned Raggett picked out hints of the [[Pixies|b6b2bb8d-54a9-491f-9607-7b546023b433]], the Louisville underground, the early Merge scene and Neil Young.

Trouser Press was more mixed: it heard Galaxie 500 and [[Codeine|cecd5f91-cfdd-45d1-879f-3920c7c76e58]] in it, liked Park's quiet songs and found the fast ones less convincing.

years.p: A 1992 seven-inch on Merge Records, the Chapel Hill label McCaughan ran with his Superchunk bandmates.

years.cap: Seam in Chicago with Lexi Mitchell
years.h: McCaughan goes back to Superchunk; Seam moves to Chicago
years.p: With McCaughan out to concentrate on [[Superchunk|61653550-fd9b-4401-8248-44f2d064d384]], Park and Mitchell relocate to Chicago. Bob Rising takes over the drums and Craig White joins on second guitar.

years.h: John McEntire drums on the Kernel sessions at Idful
years.p: Seam records four songs at Idful in Chicago with [[Brad Wood|58c8c056-4f9a-4a3b-8dd9-69b06bb23c28]] engineering. The credits list [[John McEntire|73e452bb-1f86-4dec-a2aa-a8b097fea4c6]], soon of [[Tortoise|e0953daa-860f-4dc8-9f1a-b12587cdaf17]], on drums.
years.xp: The EP mixed two new songs, an alternate take of "Shame" and a cover of Chicago band [[Breaking Circus|5f92a6ee-44ef-4eef-8b5b-1bd359b32fd4]]'s "Driving the Dynamite Truck". Trouser Press also places McEntire and his [[Bastro|cfc5b1bf-a46c-4504-bcb6-a820416a1894]] bandmate Bundy Brown in Seam's expanded Chicago lineup.

eras.title: Touch and Go, and the record emo bands learned from
eras.text: Touch and Go signed Seam and the band made its strongest case in one year: an EP in February, an album in September. The Problem with Me is the record later critics hold up as a blueprint for the first wave of 1990s emo.

years.cap: Seam at the Metro, Chicago, March 20, 1993
years.h: Kernel EP is Seam's first release on Touch and Go
years.p: Fifteen minutes, four songs, produced by the band. The move from Homestead to the Chicago label is done.

years.cap: Seam's set list, Lounge Ax, Chicago, May 8, 1993
years.src: Wikipedia: The Problem with Me · Trouser Press · AllMusic
years.h: The Problem with Me builds the tension and lets it crash
years.p: Brad Wood produces nine songs at Idful. Spin called it "completely enveloping," and Magnet heard Park's sadness and anger in restrained guitars and half-shouted vocals.
years.xp:
In his book Gimme Indie Rock, Andrew Earles wrote that the album would be hugely influential on the first wave of 1990s emo bands. Trouser Press called it home to some of Seam's best work.

AllMusic notes the shift from the debut: a little more upbeat, and built on loud-soft dynamics.

eras.title: A hiatus, a trip to Korea, a new Seam
eras.text: Mitchell's exit in spring 1994 stopped the band, and for a while it looked final. Park came back from Korea with a new bassist, a new set of songs and a growing commitment to Asian American music that went well beyond his own band.

years.h: Lexi Mitchell leaves and Seam goes quiet
years.p: The Chicago Reader wrote that the hiatus that followed had an air of permanence, and that Park turned the painful breakup with Mitchell into songs.

years.h: Park comes home from Korea with bassist William Shin
years.p: Park returns by summer's end with William Shin, a Canadian expatriate, on bass. Reg Shrader on guitar and Chris Manfrin on drums complete the band that will make Seam's last two albums.

years.src: Wikipedia: Are You Driving Me Crazy?
years.h: A deadline session at Idful with Brad Wood and Casey Rice
years.p: The new lineup records Are You Driving Me Crazy? in January. The Chicago Tribune tied the album's edge to a tumultuous year that ended in a pressure-packed recording schedule.

years.cap: Seam in a Touch and Go press photo, c. 1995
q: You'd see this sea of black-haired kids in the audience just rocking it.
years.src: Chicago Reader: Seam/Aminiature · Bandcamp Daily · Chicago Reader: Seam's Korea Move
years.h: The Ear of the Dragon tour ends at the Double Door in Chicago
years.p: Park and Shin built the tour around Ear of the Dragon, a compilation of Asian American rock bands. The last night puts Seam with aMiniature, Venus Cures All and Cub.
years.xp:
Park and Shin put the compilation together with journalist Ben Kim. The same year the three founded the Foundation for Asian American Independent Media, which went on to present annual showcases of music, art and film.

Tobin Mori, who later played with Park, told Bandcamp Daily what Seam shows looked like from the floor.

years.src: Chicago Reader: Seam/Aminiature · Wikipedia: Are You Driving Me Crazy? · Trouser Press
years.h: Are You Driving Me Crazy? turns the breakup into a record
years.p: The Chicago Reader called it a bleak statement of emotional strain, with guitars that mewl with melancholy. Seam tours it with aMiniature and [[Versus|ee7db106-6996-42a9-981d-b2d55a9b8366]].
years.xp: The Reader also said Park and company had found the Zen of the forlorn pop tune. Trouser Press thought Park was writing at his peak, even if the record lacked the turbulence of the earlier ones.

eras.title: Glacial, then Seoul
eras.text: Seam took three years over its last album and named it accordingly. Then, with one guitarist swapped for a friend from San Diego, Park did something he'd wanted to do for years: play in South Korea.

years.h: The Pace Is Glacial, made at Electrical Audio
years.p: Recorded with [[Brian Paulson|65f13d3b-ddd6-4b33-8ab7-366ee7fb63c4]] at [[Steve Albini|a4d486bd-6020-4a36-9c7d-bf5ce174bcd1]]'s studio over December 1997 and January 1998. The songs include "Nisei Fight Song" and "Intifada Driving School".
years.xp: The Chicago Tribune said Seam distilled its no-frills guitar rock into creeper melodies and haunting ruminations. The Sunday Times heard the noise at the edges of "Little Chang" and "The Prizefighters" always pulling together into a rock riff.

years.h: Reg Shrader steps out and aMiniature's John Lee steps in
years.p: Shrader didn't want to spend his spare time traveling, Park told the Chicago Reader. John Lee, newly moved from San Diego, takes his place.
years.xp: Park's words: Shrader "doesn't have a very flexible work schedule and he didn't want to spend all of his spare time traveling." With Lee in, drummer Chris Manfrin became the only member of Seam who wasn't Korean American.

years.h: Seam plays Soran in Seoul, a first for American indie rock
years.p: Two nights at a small Seoul festival whose name translates as "big sound". By the Reader's account, Seam was the first American indie band ever to play South Korea.
years.xp:
An American friend at MTV Korea set it up, and the band waded through "tons of paperwork" for permission. After the set they met a fan who said he'd spent a month in jail for coming home with a Cannibal Corpse album, and who had once worked for the government translating foreign lyrics for inspection. He said he'd edited lyrics on American records, Nirvana's In Utero among them, so they would pass.

Korean label Gang A.G. licensed The Pace Is Glacial for the shows, but the local edition didn't come out until Seam had gone home. About 200 people came the first night and about 400 the second.

years.src: AllMusic · Chicago Reader: Seam's Korea Move · Bandcamp Daily
years.p: AllMusic dates the end of Seam to 2000, after the South Korea trip. In late 1999 the band had talked about a new album for Touch and Go; no fifth album followed.
years.xp: The Korea trip left a mark on Park's next years. He and Lee met the Korean band Delispice and played on their third album, Bandcamp Daily reports.

eras.title: Ee, a film, and Panther Lau
eras.text: Park kept making music outside the Seam name and kept building the Asian American scene he'd helped start. Chris Manfrin went on to Bottomless Pit with two members of Touch and Go labelmates Silkworm.

years.h: Park's new band Ee, and songs for Better Luck Tomorrow
years.p: Ee, with Tobin Mori and Che Chou, releases For 100 We Try Harder on Asian Man Records. Park also helps director Justin Lin license songs for Better Luck Tomorrow.

years.h: Park resurfaces as Panther Lau in Bored Spies
years.p: Bored Spies put out the "Summer 720" seven-inch on Damnably. By then Park was in Singapore, going by Panther Lau.
years.xp: On living outside the US, Park told Bandcamp Daily: "My own connections to the U.S. are shallow." His parents had moved there as students.
